introduction: These readings, most of them ‘Abdu’l-Bahá's remarks in letters and table talk, look at history for what it teaches. The past is called the mirror of the future; empires, conquerors and cities are shown to have vanished while those who served God are remembered; Persia's glory and decline, the rise of the Arabs, the decay of religions through their own leaders, and the long record of war are each read as lessons; and there are notes on places, from Nineveh to Akka. A hundred of the guide's two hundred and six quotations are read here, ten from each tenth of the reading order, beside a hundred from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: the prophets on Nineveh, Babylon and Tyre, the Qur'an's 'travel in the land', Ecclesiastes, Thucydides, Marcus Aurelius on Alexander, Shelley, Gray, Byron and Kipling on the fall of the mighty. Twelve push back or add a side: the Preacher's 'no new thing', Carlyle's history of great men, the poor wise man nobody remembered, Antony on the evil that lives after us, Heraclitus on war, Montaigne on who is called barbarous, and, where the readings fault the teachers of other religions, Jesus on the mote and the beam.
questions: 'The past is the mirror of the future.' Choose one episode in these readings and say what it is meant to show.
The readings say kings are forgotten and servants of God remembered. Ecclesiastes tells of a poor wise man whom no one remembered. What does history actually keep?
Decline is traced again and again to religious leaders. How do the readings, and Jeremiah and Malachi beside them, tell the fault of leaders from the fault of a faith?
Several passages generalize about peoples and religions. Where would Jesus's mote and beam, or Montaigne on barbarism, ask for caution?
Heraclitus called war the father of all; the readings call six thousand years of it a record to end. What would it take to learn from it?
Some remarks here correct or question historical accounts. How should a reader weigh table talk as history?

outside.why: Thucydides says he wrote his history not to win the applause of the moment but as a possession for all time.
Moses' last song says: remember the days of old, consider the years of many generations; ask thy father and thy elders.
Jesus rebuked those who built the tombs of the prophets and said they would never have joined their fathers in killing them.
The Qur'an closes the story of Joseph by saying that in their history there is a lesson for men of understanding.
Proverbs says that the simple believe every word, but the prudent man looks well to his going.
Bildad tells Job to enquire of the former age, for we are but of yesterday, and know nothing.
Wilfred Owen called it the old lie, told to children ardent for glory, that it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country.
Shelley's traveller finds a shattered statue whose pedestal still commands the mighty to look on its works and despair.
The Preacher holds that there is no new thing under the sun. If so, are 'modern concepts' new at all, and does anything in history really change?
Luke begins his Gospel by saying he has traced all things from the first, to write them in order, so that the reader may know the certainty.
Zephaniah foresaw Nineveh, the rejoicing city that said 'I am, and there is none beside me', become a desolation.
Nahum has all who look on the city say: Nineveh is laid waste; who will bemoan her?
The book of Jonah tells how the prophet cried in Nineveh, and the people of Nineveh believed God.
Jesus took the story as history: the men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment, because they repented at the preaching of Jonas.
The Qur'an's account of the sleepers says, as a thing reported, that they tarried in their cave three hundred years and nine.
Genesis gives the longest of the ancient lives: all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty and nine years.
Marcus Aurelius noted that Alexander the Macedonian and his groom were brought by death to the same state.
Ecclesiastes says that one generation passes away and another comes, but the earth abides for ever.
Byron read the same cycle in history's one page: first freedom, then glory, then wealth, vice, corruption, and barbarism at last.
Isaiah says that the grass withers and the flower fades, but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
The Qur'an gives travel the same purpose: travel in the land, and see the consequence for those who were before you.
The Qur'an asks whether they have not travelled in the land, and adds that it is not the eyes that grow blind, but the hearts.
Isaiah said that Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, would never be inhabited from generation to generation.
Gray wrote in a country churchyard that the boast of heraldry and the pomp of power await the same hour: the paths of glory lead but to the grave.
Carlyle held that universal history is at bottom the history of the great men who have worked here. Whose lives, on the readings' account, does history really keep?
Proverbs says that the memory of the just is blessed, but the name of the wicked shall rot.
Isaiah taunts a fallen tyrant who said in his heart, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God.
Ecclesiastes tells of a poor wise man who saved his city, yet no man remembered him. Is it always true that service outlives kings in memory?
Hamlet imagines imperious Caesar, dead and turned to clay, stopping a hole to keep the wind away.
The Qur'an says of a vanished people: how many were the gardens and watersprings they left behind, an inheritance for other folk.
Lamentations begins with a fallen capital: how doth the city sit solitary, she that was great among the nations.
The book of Esther remembers a Persian king who reigned from India even unto Ethiopia, over a hundred and twenty-seven provinces.
Isaiah calls a Persian king, Cyrus, the Lord's anointed, before whom the gates shall not be shut.
The book of Ezra preserves the decree of Cyrus king of Persia, sending an exiled people home to rebuild.
Daniel read the writing on the wall to a king: thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians.
Isaiah has God say to a forsaken people: for a small moment have I forsaken thee, but with great mercies will I gather thee.
The exiles in Babylon sat by the rivers and wept when they remembered Zion.
Kipling warned his own country that all its pomp of yesterday is one with Nineveh and Tyre.
A psalm says that man's days are as grass: he flourishes as a flower of the field, and the wind passes over it.
Plutarch says Lycurgus found extreme inequality in Sparta, its wealth centred on a very few, and made a new division of the land.
Paul told the Athenians that God made of one blood all nations of men. Does kinship between peoples need a common stock, or does it rest on something wider?
Whitman saw the continents meant from the first to be connected: the oceans crossed, the distant brought near.
Matthew tells of wise men who came from the east to Jerusalem, having seen a star.
God tells Moses that he has come down to deliver the people and bring them to a land flowing with milk and honey.
Abraham was brought out under the night sky and told: so shall thy seed be.
Genesis records the call: get thee out of thy country and thy father's house, and I will make of thee a great nation.
Hebrews says that Abraham went out not knowing whither he went, and sojourned in the land of promise as in a strange country.
The Qur'an reminds the Arabs that they were enemies, on the brink of an abyss of fire, and were made brothers.
The Apocalypse tells an early church: I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love.
The book of Judges says that after Joshua's generation there arose another which knew not the Lord nor his works.
Ezekiel cries woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves and not the flock.
Malachi blames the priests by the measure of what a priest should be, a messenger of the Lord whose lips keep knowledge. Is the fault in the ministry, or in its betrayal?
Blake saw priests in black gowns walking their rounds, and binding with briars his joys and desires.
Jesus charged the teachers of his day with laying aside the commandment of God to hold the tradition of men.
Proverbs describes the field of the slothful, grown over with thorns, its wall broken down.
Nehemiah's companions answered him: let us rise up and build, and strengthened their hands for the work.
Jesus warned his own followers that salt which has lost its savour is good for nothing.
The Qur'an's own rule is that God does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in their hearts.
Arnold, in the nineteenth century, saw a world with neither certitude nor peace, like a darkling plain.
Jesus said that a prophet is not without honour, save in his own country and in his own house.
Paul says that God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and the weak to confound the mighty.
Jesus said of his own hearers that seeing they see not, and hearing they hear not.
The Qur'an distinguishes its clear verses from the allegorical, and says those with doubt in their hearts pursue the allegorical.
Paul says that what happened to an earlier people happened as examples, and was written for our admonition.
The charge was first made from within: Jeremiah told those who said 'the law of the Lord is with us' that the pen of the scribes is in vain.
Jesus asked why we see the mote in a brother's eye and not the beam in our own. These readings fault Jewish, Christian and Muslim teachers alike; on whom else might the charge fall?
The Qur'an observes that people have broken their religion into sects, each group rejoicing in its tenets.
Jeroboam, to keep his kingdom, made two calves of gold and told Israel: behold thy gods.
Paul met the first parties in the church with a question: is Christ divided?
Milton would let truth and falsehood grapple, sure that truth is never worsted in a free and open encounter. Is doctrinal dispute always a harm to a cause?
The Qur'an preserves the words themselves: grieve not; lo, God is with us.
Tertullian told the persecutors that the oftener Christians are mown down the more they grow: the blood of Christians is seed.
A psalm says that some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will remember the name of the Lord.
Heraclitus called war the father of all and the king of all. Is strife the engine of history, as he thought, or its long illness?
Isaiah set against that record the day when nation shall not lift up sword against nation, nor learn war any more.
Augustine wrote that peace should be the object of desire and war waged only as a necessity. Has that rule restrained the six thousand years, or excused them?
A psalm shows how early history travelled: we have heard with our ears; our fathers have told us what was done in the times of old.
Eisenhower reckoned the cost: every gun that is made is, in the final sense, a theft from those who hunger and are not fed.
The Apocalypse hears the cry over a great trading city: Babylon the great is fallen.
Proverbs gives the rule in a line: righteousness exalteth a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people.
The line between the two powers was drawn in the Gospel: render unto Caesar what is Caesar's, and unto God what is God's.
Jesus said that every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation, and no house so divided shall stand.
A psalm of exile vows: if I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning.
Joel asks that what has happened be told to the children, and by them to another generation.
This is the chapter's language: from generation to generation it shall lie waste, under the line of confusion and the stones of emptiness.
Thucydides has an envoy state the rule of conquerors: the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.
Hosea names it: I will give her the valley of Achor for a door of hope.
Ezekiel records the lament for the greatest Phoenician port: what city is like Tyrus, destroyed in the midst of the sea?
Hebrews says the patriarchs confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth, seeking a better country.
Jesus wept over Jerusalem because it did not know the things that belong to its peace. What has the land of the prophets made of its light?
The Qur'an asks: dost thou not consider how thy Lord dealt with 'Ad, with many-columned Iram, and with Thamud who clove the rocks?
The Qur'an tells how Salih was sent to the tribe of Thamud, saying: O my people, serve God.
The verse is Hosea's: when Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.
Acton drew the lesson of such reigns: power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.
Aristotle said that man perfected is the best of animals, but separated from law and justice the worst of all.
Montaigne, told of a newly found people, could find nothing barbarous in them, and thought everyone gives that title to whatever is not his own custom. Who decides what barbarism is?
The Qur'an calls victories and defeats the vicissitudes which God causes to follow one another for mankind.
A psalm resolves not to hide the past from the children, but to show the generation to come what was done.
Ecclesiastes says there is no remembrance of the wise more than of the fool; in days to come all is forgotten.
Shakespeare's Antony says that the evil men do lives after them, while the good is often interred with their bones. Is memory as just as the readings hope?

deuteronomy-remember-the-days-of-old.text: Remember the days of old, consider the years of many generations: ask thy father, and he will shew thee; thy elders, and they will tell thee

job-enquire-of-the-former-age.text: For enquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers: (For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth are a shadow

corinthians-written-for-our-admonition.text: Now all these things happened unto them for examples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come

zephaniah-rejoicing-city.text: This is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me: how is she become a desolation, a place for beasts to lie down in! every one that passeth by her shall hiss, and wag his hand

nahum-nineveh-is-laid-waste.text: And it shall come to pass, that all they that look upon thee shall flee from thee, and say, Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her? whence shall I seek comforters for thee

matthew-men-of-nineveh.text: The men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: because they repented at the preaching of Jonas; and, behold, a greater than Jonas is here

quran-in-their-history-a-lesson.text: In their history verily there is a lesson for men of understanding. It is no invented story but a confirmation of the existing (Scripture) and a detailed explanation of everything, and a guidance and a mercy for folk who believe.

quran-tarried-in-their-cave.text: And (it is said) they tarried in their Cave three hundred years and add nine.

ecclesiastes-poor-wise-man.text: There was a little city, and few men within it; and there came a great king against it, and besieged it, and built great bulwarks against it: Now there was found in it a poor wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city; yet no man remembered that same poor man

ecclesiastes-no-remembrance-of-the-wise.text: For there is no remembrance of the wise more than of the fool for ever; seeing that which now is in the days to come shall all be forgotten. And how dieth the wise man? as the fool

kings-calves-of-gold.text: Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt

hosea-out-of-egypt.text: When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt

isaiah-line-of-confusion.text: from generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it for ever and ever. But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness

esther-from-india-unto-ethiopia.text: Now it came to pass in the days of Ahasuerus, (this is Ahasuerus which reigned, from India even unto Ethiopia, over an hundred and seven and twenty provinces

hebrews-abraham-went-out.text: By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went. By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise: For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God

exodus-milk-and-honey.text: And I am come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians, and to bring them up out of that land unto a good land and a large, unto a land flowing with milk and honey

ezekiel-what-city-is-like-tyrus.text: And in their wailing they shall take up a lamentation for thee, and lament over thee, saying, What city is like Tyrus, like the destroyed in the midst of the sea

isaiah-babylon-glory-of-kingdoms.text: And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldees' excellency, shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. It shall never be inhabited, neither shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation

psalm-our-fathers-have-told-us.text: We have heard with our ears, O God, our fathers have told us, what work thou didst in their days, in the times of old

joel-tell-your-children.text: Tell ye your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation

luke-write-unto-thee-in-order.text: It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus, That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed

byron-history-hath-but-one-page.text: First Freedom, and then Glory—when that fails, / Wealth—Vice—Corruption,—Barbarism at last. / And History, with all her volumes vast, / Hath but one page
byron-history-hath-but-one-page.author: Lord Byron

thucydides-possession-for-all-time.text: I have written my work, not as an essay which is to win the applause of the moment, but as a possession for all time
thucydides-possession-for-all-time.author: Thucydides

plutarch-lycurgus-division-of-lands.text: For there was an extreme inequality amongst them, and their state was overloaded with a multitude of indigent and necessitous persons, while its whole wealth had centered upon a very few
plutarch-lycurgus-division-of-lands.author: Plutarch
plutarch-lycurgus-division-of-lands.translator: John Dryden, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough

marcus-alexander-and-his-groom.text: Alexander the Macedonian and his groom by death were brought to the same state
marcus-alexander-and-his-groom.author: Marcus Aurelius

quran-brink-of-an-abyss.text: And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate. And remember Allah's favour unto you: How ye were enemies and He made friendship between your hearts so that ye became as brothers by His grace; and (how) ye were upon the brink of an abyss of fire, and He did save you from it. Thus Allah maketh clear His revelations unto you, that haply ye may be guided,
